newsitem.title: USA: US House Ag panel approves new 1-yr CRP contracts.
newsitem.headline: US House Ag panel approves new 1-yr CRP contracts.

text.p: The House Agriculture Committee overwhelmingly approved Thursday a new one-year Conservation Reserve Program contract for farmers with fall-planted crops.

The measure would provide a one-year contract for producers of fall-planted crops whose CRP contracts are expiring, and who signed up last month for the government's new program, but have not yet been notified by the Agriculture Department if their acres were accepted.

For producers bidding into the program, there would be a new contract with new rental rates, a committee staffer said. The rental rates would vary regionally, but would generally be lower than current rates.
If the farmer's acreage is then accepted into CRP, the farmers would automatically go into the 10-year program, in effect nullifying the one-year agreement.
The legislation was prompted by concern that the USDA would bungle a massive turnover of land in the reserve. Contracts on some 21 million acres expire this fall.
The bill approved by the committee could affect several million acres, according to informal estimates.
A spokesman for chairman Bob Smith, Oregon Republican, sponsor of the bill, said Smith hoped to arrange a floor vote soon.

There were obstacles in the way of enactment. No hearings on the bill were scheduled in the Senate Agriculture Committee, where chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, has opposed extension of CRP contracts.
Agriculture Secrtary Dan Glickman also has been unenthusiastic about extensions.

During their two-hour bill-drafting session, House committee members approved an amendment allowing farmers to withdraw land from the Conservation Reserve as early as July 1 without any reduction in their rental payment for 1997.
At present, farmers can begin field preparation for new crops 90 days before expiration of their contracts without penalty.

Smith called his bill "a technical fix that will allow winter crop producers to know now they have a (Conservation Reserve) contract for the coming crop year." Under it, farmers who submitted bids to enroll land in the reserve could unilaterally claim an extension if they notified USDA during a special period called by USDA.
